caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was gypsum, carved to order.

In 1868 a New York tobacconist named George Hull, with H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry a block of gypsum ten feet four and a half inches long at Fort Dodge, Iowa. He told them it was for a Lincoln monument in New York. In Chicago, stonecutter Edward Burkhardt's sculptors Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann cut it into a man modelled on Hull himself. Quilts were hung to muffle the sound. Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles aged the surface and gave it pores. A geologist told Hull hair would not petrify, so the figure was made hairless.

It was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in Cardiff, New York, in late November 1868. Nearly a year later, on 16 October 1869, hired well-diggers found it. Newell charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people came a day.

Andrew D. White of Cornell noticed the well had been sunk where no well was needed: the farm already had a good spring. Yale's O. C. Marsh saw fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum and called it "a most decided humbug". Hull confessed on 10 December 1869, saying he wanted to show how easily people believe.

Still unresolved: whether Burkhardt understood what he was carving is not clear. And the giant P. T. Barnum had copied in wax is only claimed, by its owner, to be the one in a Michigan arcade museum.

Images: the lithograph "The Onondaga Giant" (Popular Graphic Arts); a Bain News Service negative of the giant, 1910; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa. All public domain.

cards.headline: Ten feet of stone, <y>sold as a fossil man</y>
cards.note: Exhumed at Cardiff, Onondaga County, New York, 16 October 1869.
cards.alt: Lithograph showing two views of a large stone man lying on a low plinth.

cards.headline: The well was dug <y>where no well was needed</y>
cards.note: Andrew D. White of Cornell inspected the pit closely. The spot was convenient to neither the house nor the barn, and a good spring and stream already ran to both. He called the whole matter a hoax.
cards.alt: Pale stone figure lying in an earth pit, hand-labelled Cardiff Giant on the negative.

cards.headline: The quarrymen were told <y>it was for Lincoln</y>
cards.note: In 1868 George Hull and H. B. Martin hired men to cut a gypsum block ten feet four and a half inches long at Fort Dodge, Iowa, saying it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.
cards.source: Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, 1873 · public domain
cards.alt: Sepia view of a pale rock face in a wooded quarry above broken stone blocks.

cards.headline: By 1873 the printed caption <y>named both men</y>
cards.note: The back of this souvenir card sets out the route: block taken from the gypsum quarry to Chicago, the giant carved, then shipped to New York, buried in a barn lot and subsequently "discovered". The perpetrators, it says, were George Hull and H. B. Martin.
cards.source: Stereocard verso, Cardiff Glen, 1873 · public domain
cards.alt: Printed text on the back of an old stereocard, headed View in Cardiff Glen.

cards.headline: Nose, six inches. <y>Printed as measurement, not sculpture</y>
cards.note: The sheet lists him like a specimen: whole length 10 feet 4½ inches, mouth 4 inches, palm 7 inches. Yale's O. C. Marsh looked at the object instead and found fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum. He called it a most decided humbug.
cards.alt: Printed dimensions listed beneath the title The Onondaga Giant on an old sheet.

cards.headline: Two sculptors carved it. <y>Did their employer know?</y>
cards.note: Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann did the cutting for Chicago stonecutter Edward Burkhardt, behind hung quilts that lessened the sound. Whether Burkhardt understood what Hull intended it for is still not clear. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869; both giants were declared fakes in court on 2 February 1870.
cards.alt: Close view of the stone figure's hairless head and shoulder lying in dark soil.
